name: BRIGHT LEEKS, BIG CITY BURGER (comes with grilled leeks)

recipe.history: The leek — Allium ampeloprasum — is an ancient vegetable with roots in the Mediterranean basin and the Near East, cultivated for at least four thousand years and carrying within its long history a significance that far exceeds its modest role as a flavoring agent. The Egyptians were devoted to leeks — archaeological evidence from the time of the Pharaohs includes murals depicting leek cultivation and records of leeks being fed to the workers who built the pyramids at Giza, who apparently consumed them in such quantities that their cost appears in administrative accounts alongside beer and bread. The Sumerians and Babylonians cultivated leeks, and ancient Greek and Roman physicians prescribed them for throat ailments and as a general tonic. Emperor Nero of Rome was reportedly so passionate about leeks — believing they improved the quality of his singing voice — that he earned the mocking nickname Porrophagus, the leek-eater. The leek became and remains the national symbol of Wales, associated by legend with the Battle of Heathfield in 633 CE, when Welsh soldiers wore leeks in their helmets to distinguish themselves from their Saxon enemies. Unlike the onion, which cooks down to sweetness and softness, or the garlic, which loses its sharp edge in long cooking, the leek maintains a gentle, grassy, almost sweet allium flavor throughout any preparation — it is the most refined member of its family, the one best suited to long, gentle heat that coaxes out its subtle character.
recipe.history2: Leeks arrived in American cooking primarily through the French culinary tradition — the leek is foundational to French cuisine in a way it never quite became in British or German cooking, despite its popularity in Wales. Vichyssoise, the cold leek and potato soup, was invented (or popularized) in New York City at the Ritz-Carlton around 1917 by chef Louis Diat, who named it after the French town near his birthplace. This gave the leek a certain glamour in American fine dining that it retained through the twentieth century, associated with sophisticated French-inspired cooking rather than everyday American kitchens. Grilled leeks, however — halved lengthwise and charred over high heat until the exterior leaves are blackened and the interior becomes molten and sweet — represent a more democratic and direct treatment that belongs to the American backyard grill tradition as much as to any European kitchen. The grill transforms the leek entirely: the outer layers blacken and smoke, and the interior, protected and steamed by those charred leaves, becomes silky, sweet, and deeply caramelized. Split open, seasoned with vinaigrette or simply with flaky salt and good olive oil, a grilled leek placed on a hamburger is a revelation of textural contrast and layered allium sweetness.
recipe.history3_personal: I did not grow up eating leeks. They were not a vegetable that appeared in my childhood home, which ran to carrots, onions, and potatoes — the sturdy, cooperative alliums that didn't require explanation or special handling. Leeks entered my life late, in my mid-twenties, when I was cooking my way through a French cookbook of the kind that takes itself very seriously and uses the word "rustic" to mean technically demanding. The first dish was a leek vinaigrette — leeks poached whole until tender, dressed while still warm with a Dijon-sharpened vinaigrette and scattered with chopped hard-boiled egg. It was a revelation of simplicity and elegance, the leek so soft and yielding it almost dissolved against the tongue, the vinaigrette cutting through its sweetness with precision. I became a leek enthusiast immediately, in the way you become enthusiastic about something you've overlooked for years and can't quite believe you missed. The grilled preparation came later and cemented my devotion: a leek cut in half lengthwise, laid over charcoal until the outside is black and terrifying-looking, then opened to reveal a yielding, caramelized interior that tastes like the best version of an onion that ever existed. I have been putting grilled leeks on things ever since — flatbreads, pastas, and, finally, the burger it was always destined for.
recipe.history4_philosophy: Grilled leeks on a hamburger are an argument about temperature and transformation: the leek must be warm, even hot, still carrying the smokiness of the grill, to do its work properly against the beef. And the beef, in turn, must be at medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — to be the right partner for a vegetable as generous and complex as a properly grilled leek. The leek's sweetness needs the iron and the fat of the beef to ground it; without that richness, it can seem almost too gentle, too sweet, unmoored. The beef's richness needs the leek's grassy, slightly smoky sweetness to provide relief and contrast; without it, the burger is satisfying but one-dimensional. Medium rare ensures the beef is still juicy and fat-rich, ensuring that every bite includes both the leek's softness and the patty's yielding, pink, juice-filled interior. To cook the patty to well done is to remove the richness that makes the leek's sweetness meaningful, to strip the dish of its central tension. The combination only works at the right temperature. That temperature is medium rare, and there is no substitute.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
4 medium leeks, dark green tops trimmed, roots trimmed
For the leek vinaigrette (for dressing the grilled leeks):
120ml crème fraîche or full-fat sour cream
Salt and white pepper to taste
4 thin slices quality prosciutto or jambon de Paris
instructions: 1. Prepare the leeks for grilling: Trim the leeks, removing root ends and dark green tops, leaving the pale white and light green portions. Halve each leek lengthwise, cutting all the way through. Rinse under cold running water, fanning the layers gently to remove any grit. Pat thoroughly dry with paper towels. Brush cut sides and exterior generously with olive oil, season with salt and pepper.

2. Grill the leeks: Heat a grill or grill pan over high heat until very hot. Place leeks cut-side down on the grates. Grill without moving for 4–5 minutes until deeply charred and caramelized on the cut side. Flip and grill on the rounded exterior side for another 3–4 minutes, until the outer leaves are blackened and the interior feels soft when pressed. Transfer to a cutting board. Once cool enough to handle, peel away any heavily charred outer leaves to reveal the tender, caramelized interior. Slice the grilled leek halves into 2-inch sections.

3. Dress the grilled leeks: Whisk together Dijon mustard, red wine vinegar, and honey. Stream in olive oil while whisking to emulsify. Add minced tarragon and season with salt and pepper. Toss warm grilled leek pieces in the vinaigrette. Let sit at room temperature until needed.

4. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low 2 minutes, then medium 4 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Once fully incorporated, mix on medium-high 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Rise in a covered, oiled bowl for 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

5. Divide bun dough into 4 portions, shape into tight balls, place on parchment-lined baking sheet, and flatten gently. Proof covered 45–60 minutes. Brush with egg wash and bake at 375°F / 190°C for 15–18 minutes until golden. Cool completely.
6. Make the Dijon cream spread: Combine crème fraîche, whole-grain Dijon, lemon juice, and grated garlic. Stir until uniform. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 225g each). Press into round patties 3/4 inch thick and 4 inches wide. Press a dimple in the center of each. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat for 3 minutes until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the skillet, leaving space between them. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes.

9. Flip once. Place a slice of Gruyère on each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes, covering the pan in the last minute to melt the cheese. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. Remove and rest on a wire rack 3–4 minutes.
10. Warm prosciutto: Lay prosciutto slices in a dry skillet over medium-high heat for 1 minute per side until lightly crisped. Set aside.
11. Toast the buns: Slice buns and toast cut-side down in a lightly buttered skillet over medium heat until golden, 1–2 minutes.

12. Assemble: Spread Dijon cream generously on both bun halves. Add frisée or watercress to the bottom bun. Place the rested cheese-topped patty on the greens. Arrange a generous pile of dressed grilled leeks over the patty. Add crisped prosciutto over the leeks. Close with the top bun and serve immediately while the leeks are still warm.
